notes.h: Land-use zones in the modern city
notes.b: A large city is divided into zones of land use. Each zone has its own pattern of buildings and activity, and its own land value. The zones below are typical of a large European city and can all be identified in Dublin.
points: CBD (central business district): the commercial heart of the city, with the highest land values, tall buildings and the most intensive use of land.
Zone in transition: the inner-city area of mixed old housing, warehouses and small industry, where decay and renewal exist side by side.
Inner residential zone: older terraced housing close to the centre.
Suburbs: lower-density housing, mainly semi-detached houses, built later and further from the centre.
Industrial zones: the port, inner-city industry, suburban industrial estates and business parks.
Open space and recreation: parks, playing fields and other green areas within the built-up city.
Transport land: roads, railway lines, the port and the airport.
Rural-urban fringe: the transitional land at the edge of the built-up area, where urban and rural land uses meet and compete.
Land values are highest here because accessibility is greatest, so the most valuable sites are used for the most profitable activities.
Tall buildings maximise the use of expensive land, with several floors of offices or shops on a small site.
Department stores, chain stores and specialist shops occupy the main shopping streets.
Offices, banks and the head offices of companies cluster together in the centre.
Government and cultural buildings are located in the centre, where they are most accessible.
Few people live in the CBD, so it is crowded during the working day and quiet at night.
Pedestrian streets are used in the busiest shopping areas, where traffic and crowds would otherwise congest the streets.
Vertical zoning: shops occupy the ground floor, with offices or other uses above.

Dublin's CBD lies on both sides of the River Liffey. Its main shopping streets are Grafton Street, south of the Liffey, and Henry Street, north of it, both pedestrianised, and O'Connell Street, the city's main street.

notes.b: Three models describe how land uses arrange themselves around a city centre. Each is a simplified generalisation, so it is judged by how well it fits the real city.
points: Burgess concentric zone model: Ernest Burgess, 1925, based on Chicago. Land uses form rings around the CBD, with land values and densities falling with distance from the centre.

Strength of the Burgess model: it shows the regular fall in land value and density outwards from the CBD. Limitation: it ignores transport routes and does not fit cities whose growth follows roads and rail lines.
Diagram: concentric rings drawn around a central point labelled CBD, with the zones of transition, residential and commuter land shown in turn.
Hoyt sector model: Homer Hoyt, 1939. Land uses extend outwards in wedge-shaped sectors along transport routes, and a high-class residential sector lies away from industry.
Strength of the Hoyt model: it explains why sectors of the city are elongated along roads, rail lines and rivers. Limitation: it does not show the separate suburban centres that grow in large cities.
Diagram: a circle divided into wedge-shaped sectors, with radial transport routes marked and the high-class residential sector shown away from the industrial sector.

Harris and Ullman multiple nuclei model: Chauncy Harris and Edward Ullman, 1945. A city grows around several separate centres, such as the CBD, suburban shopping centres, an airport and business parks.
Strength of the multiple nuclei model: it explains the growth of suburban centres. Limitation: it gives no simple pattern of rings or sectors, so it is less clear as a general description.
Diagram: a city outline with several separate centres marked, each surrounded by its own cluster of land use.

Dublin fits the multiple nuclei and sector models better than the concentric model: the CBD is one nucleus, while suburban shopping centres and business parks are other nuclei, and growth follows the main roads out of the city.

notes.b: Dublin shows the zones of a modern European city, with the inner city in transition and the outer city growing along the M50 and the western new towns.
points: Georgian core: the Georgian squares, Merrion Square and Fitzwilliam Square, are now largely offices.
The Wide Streets Commissioners, set up in 1757, widened and improved the city's streets, shaping the centre's wide thoroughfares.
Inner-city docklands and the north inner city are in transition, with older industrial and port land being renewed.
Older inner suburbs lie between the centre and the outer suburbs, with older housing forming an inner residential zone.
Outer suburbs and the western new towns: Tallaght, Clondalkin, Lucan and Blanchardstown, planned in the Wright Report of 1967.
Business and industrial parks lie near the M50 and the N7: Grange Castle, Citywest, Park West and Sandyford.
The port and airport are major transport and industrial land uses: Dublin Port and Dublin Airport.

Open space includes Phoenix Park, about 700 hectares and one of Europe's largest enclosed city parks, established in 1662; the Dublin Mountains and Dublin Bay are further open spaces at the edge of the city.

notes.b: Paris is the world city studied for comparison. Its land uses are concentrated in the inner city and organised around a ring road and a set of outer business and housing areas.
points: The City of Paris has about 2.1 million people on about 105 km², divided into 20 arrondissements. The wider Île-de-France region has about 12 million people.
The CBD and government quarter lie in the inner arrondissements.
Haussmann's boulevards: Haussmann rebuilt central Paris between 1853 and 1870, creating wide boulevards that give the inner city its formal street pattern.
La Défense, west of the city, is one of Europe's largest purpose-built business districts, an office district outside the historic inner city.
The Boulevard Périphérique, completed in 1973, is the ring road that forms the boundary of the inner city.
The banlieues are the suburbs beyond the Périphérique, where grands ensembles (large public housing estates built in the 1950s to 1970s) are found, for example Sarcelles.
The 1965 regional plan created five new towns: Cergy-Pontoise, Évry, Marne-la-Vallée, Melun-Sénart and Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines.

notes.b: Industry has moved out of the inner city to the edge, where land is cheaper and road access is better.
points: Old inner-city industry beside the port, canals and railways included brewing, biscuit-making and distilling.
Many of these sites closed or moved to suburban industrial estates and business parks near motorways.

Reasons for the move: lack of space for expansion in the inner city, cheaper land on the edge, road access for lorries, less congestion, planning policy, and new industries needing clean, modern sites.
The vacated inner-city sites are brownfield land (land previously developed, now available for reuse), which can then be redeveloped for other uses.
The Guinness brewery is an exception, having stayed at St James's Gate since Arthur Guinness's lease of 1759.
Jacob's biscuit factory moved from Bishop Street in the inner city to Tallaght in the 1970s. The old factory now houses the National Archives.
Paris: Renault's Boulogne-Billancourt plant closed in 1992, an example of industry leaving the inner city.
Inner-city tenements (old multi-occupied houses) were cleared in the 20th century, and their residents were moved to new suburbs and new towns.
Growth of suburban housing spread the city outwards, with sprawl into commuter counties.
The trend has been reversed in places, with a return to inner-city apartment living in areas such as the Docklands, through regeneration.
Issues raised by residential change: the density of housing, the height of buildings and the social mix of the area.
Suburban shopping centres and retail parks have been built beside motorway junctions, where there is car access, free parking and cheaper land.
The Square, Tallaght, opened in 1990; Blanchardstown Centre in 1996; Liffey Valley in 1998; and Dundrum Town Centre in 2005. All are beside major roads or the M50.
Out-of-town office parks have been built in the same way, on sites with good road access.
Effects on the city centre: vacant units and lost trade as shoppers move to the edge.
Responses: pedestrianisation of the centre, regeneration of central streets and limits on the size of retail parks.
Paris: La Défense takes offices out of the inner city, while the suburban business districts of the region take other commercial uses.
Zoning: planning authorities divide land into use zones through development plans to control where each use may be located.
Brownfield and greenfield development: reuse of old urban land must be balanced against building on undeveloped edge land.
Height and density: taller and denser buildings in the centre raise questions of design, light and services.
Transport: new zones must be linked to public transport, or they generate car journeys and congestion.
Mixed land use: combining housing, offices and shops in one area reduces travel but can cause conflict between uses.
Conflict between business, residents and heritage: new offices or roads can threaten housing or historic buildings.

notes.b: Bid-rent theory, put forward by William Alonso in 1964, explains why land values and land uses change with distance from the centre. Bid-rent is the most a user can afford to pay for a plot of land.
points: Accessibility is greatest at the centre, so competition for sites is fiercest there and land is dearest at the peak land value intersection (PLVI), the point of highest value.
Land values fall with distance from the centre, because each step outwards means less accessibility.
Commerce outbids industry for central sites, and industry outbids housing, because each use can pay a different amount for the same land.
Secondary peaks of land value form at suburban centres, ring-road junctions and along main roads, where accessibility is also high.
Effect on building: tall buildings and intensive use occur at the centre, while large, low-density uses such as warehouses and car parks occur at the edge.

notes.b: Social stratification is the division of a city's population into groups by income, class, ethnicity, age and family stage, and segregation is the separation of these groups into different areas.
points: Causes: land and house prices, the allocation of social housing, planning decisions, transport access, household choice and discrimination.
Results: affluent areas are set against areas of concentrated disadvantage, and gated developments create closed residential areas.

Gentrification: better-off people move into and renovate a poorer inner-city area, raising prices and displacing lower-income residents. It is a different process from urban renewal and redevelopment, which are covered in the note Urban planning and renewal.
Dublin: affluent south-east suburbs, including Ballsbridge, Donnybrook, Dalkey and Foxrock, contrast with lower-income areas in parts of the north inner city and in some outer social-housing estates.
Ballymun is the case of concentrated social housing in Dublin, with seven 15-storey tower blocks built between 1966 and 1969.
Gentrification around the Docklands: the inner-city area has attracted new residents and businesses, including Google's European headquarters at Grand Canal Dock, known as 'Silicon Docks'.
Paris: the wealthy western districts contrast with the poorer north-eastern banlieues of Seine-Saint-Denis, the poorest département in mainland France.
Immigrant residents are concentrated in grands ensembles, and the riots that began in Clichy-sous-Bois in October 2005 showed the tensions in these areas.

notes.h: Expansion of cities and pressure on rural land
notes.b: As cities grow, they take in rural land at the rural-urban fringe. The pressures on rural land are caused by population growth and by the choices made by households and firms.
points: Causes: population growth and in-migration; demand for cheaper, larger houses; car ownership and motorways; high house prices in the city; and jobs moving to the suburbs.
Loss of farmland: housing, roads and business parks replace fields, and rising land prices encourage farmers to sell.
Hobby farms and horse paddocks spread across the fringe, taking land out of commercial farming.
Commuter villages gain new estates, and their character and community can be lost as their population changes.
Other uses on the fringe: retail parks, business parks, data centres, landfill sites, quarries and golf courses.
Environmental effects: loss of habitats and hedgerows, and flooding as paved surfaces replace soil that would absorb rainwater.
Conflicts between farmers, residents and developers over the future of the fringe.
Dublin: sprawl into Meath, Kildare and Wicklow. The Greater Dublin Area had about 2.1 million people at the Census of 2022, about 40% of the State.
Dublin: commuter towns Navan, Ashbourne, Naas, Newbridge, Maynooth, Bray and Greystones, with one-off housing across the commuter belt.
Dublin: data centres on the city edge used about a fifth of Ireland's metered electricity in 2023 (CSO), most of them in the Dublin region.
Green belts: London's Metropolitan Green Belt was protected from the 1940s and 1950s to stop the outward sprawl of London.
New towns: Britain's New Towns Act 1946 led to Stevenage, the first new town designated, in 1946, and Milton Keynes, designated in 1967.
Paris's five new towns, from the 1965 plan, took population growth away from the city.
Dublin's western new towns of Tallaght, Clondalkin, Lucan and Blanchardstown were planned after the Wright Report of 1967.
Compact growth and brownfield targets, set out in the National Planning Framework, aim to build on land within existing settlements (see the note Urban planning and renewal).
Development plans zone land for particular uses, so that the authorities decide where expansion may take place.

keyTerms.definition: The commercial heart of a city, with the highest land values, tall buildings and the most intensive land use.
The inner-city area of mixed old housing, warehouses and small industry, where decay and renewal exist side by side.
The transitional land at the edge of a city, where urban and rural land uses meet and compete.
Burgess's 1925 model of a city as rings of land use around the CBD, based on Chicago.
Hoyt's 1939 model of a city as wedge-shaped sectors of land use extending along transport routes.
Harris and Ullman's 1945 model of a city growing around several separate centres.
Alonso's 1964 theory that land is used by the activity that can pay most for it, so value falls with distance from the centre.
The point of highest land value, usually at the centre of the city.
Previously developed urban land, often vacant or derelict, that is available for reuse.
The process by which better-off people move into and renovate a poorer inner-city area, displacing lower-income residents.
The separation of residential groups by income, class, ethnicity, age or family stage into different areas of a city.
A protected ring of open land around a city, used to prevent its outward spread.

factCards.term: The CBD: characteristics to describe
factCards.definition: Highest land values; tall buildings; department and specialist stores; offices, banks and head offices; government and cultural buildings; few residents, so busy by day and quiet at night; pedestrian streets; vertical zoning: shops below, offices above.

factCards.term: Urban land-use models: one strength and one limitation of each
factCards.definition: Burgess: shows land value and density falling outwards, but ignores transport routes. Hoyt: explains sectors along roads, rail and rivers, but misses suburban centres. Multiple nuclei: explains suburban centres, but gives no simple pattern.

factCards.term: How Dublin fits the three urban land-use models
factCards.definition: Dublin fits the multiple nuclei and sector models better than concentric rings: the CBD is one nucleus, suburban shopping centres and business parks are others, and growth follows the main roads out of the city.

factCards.term: Dublin's land-use zones: CBD and inner city
factCards.definition: CBD on both sides of the Liffey: Grafton Street (south) and Henry Street (north), both pedestrianised, and O'Connell Street. Georgian core of Merrion and Fitzwilliam Squares now largely offices. Docklands and north inner city in transition and renewal.

factCards.term: Dublin's land-use zones: outer city, industry and open space
factCards.definition: Western new towns Tallaght, Clondalkin, Lucan, Blanchardstown (Wright Report 1967); business parks near the M50 and N7: Grange Castle, Citywest, Park West, Sandyford; Dublin Port and Airport; Phoenix Park (about 700 hectares, 1662).

factCards.term: Paris: size and the pattern of its land-use zones
factCards.definition: City of Paris: about 2.1 million on about 105 km², 20 arrondissements, CBD and government in the inner ones; Haussmann's boulevards (1853–1870); La Défense offices to the west; Périphérique (1973) rings the inner city; banlieues with grands ensembles.

factCards.term: Industry moving out of the inner city: reasons
factCards.definition: Lack of space to expand; cheaper land on the edge; road access for lorries; less congestion; planning policy; new industries need clean, modern sites. The vacated inner-city sites become brownfield land for redevelopment.

factCards.term: Industrial land-use change: Jacob's, Guinness and Renault
factCards.definition: Jacob's biscuit factory moved from Bishop Street to Tallaght in the 1970s; its old factory houses the National Archives. Guinness, an exception, has stayed at St James's Gate since 1759. Paris: Renault's Boulogne-Billancourt plant closed in 1992.

factCards.term: Residential land use: three stages of change in Dublin
factCards.definition: Inner-city tenements were cleared in the 20th century and residents moved to new suburbs and new towns; suburbs sprawled into commuter counties; now a return to inner-city apartments in areas such as the Docklands. Issues: density, height, social mix.

factCards.term: Dublin's suburban shopping centres: names and opening dates
factCards.definition: The Square, Tallaght, 1990; Blanchardstown Centre, 1996; Liffey Valley, 1998; Dundrum Town Centre, 2005. All are beside major roads or the M50, for car access, free parking and cheaper land.

factCards.term: Commercial land use moving out: effects on the city centre and responses
factCards.definition: Effects: vacant units and lost trade as shoppers move to the edge. Responses: pedestrianisation, regeneration of central streets and limits on the size of retail parks. Offices also move to out-of-town office parks and, in Paris, to La Défense.

factCards.term: Planning issues raised by land-use change
factCards.definition: Zoning through development plans; brownfield versus greenfield development; building height and density; linking new zones to public transport; mixing land uses; conflict between business, residents and heritage.

factCards.term: Bid-rent theory: how land values and uses change across a city
factCards.definition: Land is dearest at the most accessible point, the PLVI, and falls with distance; commerce outbids industry, which outbids housing; secondary peaks at suburban centres, ring-road junctions and main roads; tall buildings at the centre, low density at the edge.

factCards.term: Social segregation in cities: causes and results
factCards.definition: Causes: land and house prices, social housing allocation, planning decisions, transport access, household choice and discrimination. Results: affluent areas set against areas of concentrated disadvantage; gated developments; gentrification of inner-city areas.

factCards.term: Social stratification in Dublin: three examples
factCards.definition: Affluent south-east suburbs (Ballsbridge, Donnybrook, Dalkey, Foxrock) versus lower-income parts of the north inner city and some outer estates; Ballymun's seven 15-storey towers (1966–69), concentrated social housing; gentrification in the Docklands, with Google at Grand Canal Dock.

factCards.term: Social stratification in Paris: contrasts and the 2005 riots
factCards.definition: Wealthy western districts against the poorer north-eastern banlieues of Seine-Saint-Denis, the poorest département in mainland France; immigrants concentrated in grands ensembles; riots began in Clichy-sous-Bois in October 2005.

factCards.term: Urban expansion: five causes
factCards.definition: Population growth and in-migration; demand for cheaper, larger houses; car ownership and motorways; high house prices in the city; jobs moving to the suburbs.

factCards.term: Pressures on rural land at the rural-urban fringe
factCards.definition: Farmland lost as rising prices push farmers to sell; hobby farms and horse paddocks; commuter villages gain estates and lose character; retail and business parks, data centres, landfill, quarries, golf courses; lost hedgerows and habitats; flooding.

factCards.term: Dublin's expansion: sprawl, commuter towns and data centres
factCards.definition: Sprawl into Meath, Kildare and Wicklow; GDA about 2.1 million in 2022, about 40% of the State; commuter towns Navan, Ashbourne, Naas, Newbridge, Maynooth, Bray, Greystones; data centres used about a fifth of Ireland's metered electricity in 2023.

factCards.term: Responses to urban expansion: green belts and new towns, with dates
factCards.definition: London's Metropolitan Green Belt, protected from the 1940s–50s; Britain's New Towns Act 1946: Stevenage first (1946), Milton Keynes (1967); Paris's five new towns from the 1965 plan; Dublin's western new towns; compact growth and brownfield targets in the NPF.

questions.prompt: As cities grow and expand they impact on the surrounding rural areas. Discuss, with reference to examples you have studied.
questions.model: Introduction: as a city grows, its built-up area takes in farmland and habitats at the rural-urban fringe, and the effects reach the communities beyond it. 1. Population growth and in-migration create demand for land. 2. Cheaper, larger houses and high house prices in the city push households to the edge. 3. Car ownership and motorways make long commutes possible. 4. Jobs moving to the suburbs draw people outwards. 5. Loss of farmland: housing, roads and business parks replace fields, and rising land prices encourage farmers to sell. 6. Hobby farms and horse paddocks take land out of commercial farming. 7. Commuter villages gain new estates and can lose their character and community. 8. Retail parks, business parks, data centres, landfill and quarries take further land. 9. Golf courses and other recreation use fringe land. 10. Loss of habitats and hedgerows. 11. Paved surfaces increase flooding. 12. Dublin example: sprawl into Meath, Kildare and Wicklow; the Greater Dublin Area had about 2.1 million people at the Census of 2022, about 40% of the State. 13. Dublin commuter towns Navan, Ashbourne, Naas, Newbridge, Maynooth, Bray and Greystones show the pattern. 14. Data centres on the city edge used about a fifth of Ireland's metered electricity in 2023, most in the Dublin region. 15. Responses: London's Metropolitan Green Belt, protected from the 1940s and 1950s to stop outward sprawl; Britain's New Towns Act 1946 and Stevenage, the first new town designated in 1946; Paris's five new towns from the 1965 plan; Dublin's western new towns planned after the Wright Report of 1967. Conclusion: responses take pressure off rural land only where they are enforced and where new settlements are linked to jobs and transport.

questions.prompt: Examine how land values influence land use and social stratification in cities.
questions.model: 1. Bid-rent theory (Alonso, 1964): accessibility is greatest at the centre, so competition makes land dearest at the peak land value intersection. 2. Land values fall with distance from the centre. 3. Commerce outbids industry, and industry outbids housing, so each use occupies the zone where it can pay most. 4. Secondary peaks of land value form at suburban centres, ring-road junctions and along main roads. 5. Effects on building: tall buildings and intensive use at the centre; large, low-density uses at the edge. 6. Social stratification follows land and house prices, so residential areas separate by income, class, ethnicity, age and family stage. 7. Causes of segregation include land and house prices, social housing allocation, planning, transport access, household choice and discrimination. 8. Results: affluent areas are set against areas of concentrated disadvantage, and gated developments close off residential areas. 9. Dublin: affluent south-east suburbs such as Ballsbridge, Donnybrook, Dalkey and Foxrock contrast with lower-income areas in parts of the north inner city and some outer social-housing estates. 10. Ballymun shows concentrated social housing, with seven 15-storey towers built 1966 to 1969. 11. Gentrification around the Docklands raises prices and displaces lower-income residents. 12. Paris: the wealthy western districts contrast with the north-eastern banlieues of Seine-Saint-Denis, the poorest département in mainland France. 13. Immigrant residents are concentrated in grands ensembles, and the Clichy-sous-Bois riots of October 2005 showed the tensions. Conclusion: land values sort land uses by distance from the centre, and the same market forces sort people by income into different parts of the city.

questions.model: Urban area: Dublin. Industrial land use: 1. Old inner-city industry beside the port, canals and railways, including brewing, biscuit-making and distilling, closed or moved out. 2. Reasons: lack of space, cheaper land on the edge, road access for lorries, less congestion, planning policy and the need for clean modern sites. 3. The Guinness brewery at St James's Gate is an exception, having stayed there since Arthur Guinness's lease of 1759. 5. The vacated inner-city sites are brownfield land, which can be redeveloped. Commercial land use: 6. Suburban shopping centres and retail parks were built beside motorway junctions, with car access, free parking and cheaper land. 7. The Square, Tallaght, opened in 1990; Blanchardstown Centre in 1996; Liffey Valley in 1998; Dundrum Town Centre in 2005; all beside major roads or the M50. 8.
